caseStudies.title: Cutting Application LCP from 7.0s to 1.2s & Grounded RAG Legal AI
caseStudies.summary: Transformed an unoptimized legal tech application with a 7-second LCP into a sub-1.2s engine, paired with a grounded RAG assistant that eliminated legal hallucinations.

sections.problem: DigiLawyer AI's web application suffered from a 7.0-second Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), causing steep bounce rates on legal consultation and e-Stamp acquisition funnels. Simultaneously, early prototypes of the AI legal assistant produced ungrounded answers (~30% accuracy) with high hallucination risk—unacceptable in a legal compliance domain.
rootCause: Bundle Bloat on Initial Load: Eager top-level imports forced every landing-page visitor to download heavy document editors, PDF renderers, and consultation modules before the hero painted.
Render-Blocking Assets: Unprioritized fonts, scripts, and unoptimized hero media stalled main-thread hydration.
Ungrounded LLM Prompts: Naive prompt-only generation lacked structured statutory context, leading to fabricated legal citations.
sections.architecture: Moved marketing and SEO-critical legal service pages to Next.js Static Site Generation (SSG) while keeping authenticated user workflows dynamically rendered. Deferred non-critical modals, e-Stamp workflows, and traffic challan modules behind React.lazy and next/dynamic boundaries. Replaced blocking REST responses with a grounded Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline streaming tokens over Server-Sent Events (SSE).
sections.implementation:
1. Implemented route-level code splitting separating client consultation tools from the core viewport.
2. Built an event-driven lead deduplication layer that prevented duplicate consultation submissions from rapid double-clicks and network retries.
3. Configured an SSE streaming client with custom backpressure buffers, rendering citations as verified Markdown chips directly in the chat stream.
results: 7.0s → 1.2s LCP (82% faster initial load on the core application)
+30% LCP improvement across public marketing and acquisition pages
30% → 90%+ response accuracy and 40% reduction in hallucinations on the RAG legal assistant
sections.lessons: In legal and compliance software, latency and precision are directly tied to trust. Dynamic hydration budgets and progressive streaming provide far better UX than synchronous waiting states.

caseStudies.title: Slashing Redundant API Calls by 70% & Monolith-to-Micro-Frontend Migration
caseStudies.summary: Architected a server-state caching layer using TanStack Query to eliminate duplicate compliance requests and led the strangler migration from Vue.js to React micro-frontends.

sections.problem: Enterprise compliance analysts use the FrankieOne Portal all day to review KYC/KYB verifications, AML alerts, fraud cases, comments, and custom views. Multiple sibling widgets fetched identical entity endpoints simultaneously on mount and tab switch, hammering backend compliance APIs and degrading response times. Furthermore, a legacy monolithic repo mixing Vue.js KYB modules with React modules slowed deployments and increased regression risk.
rootCause: Fragmented Fetching: Component trees relied on local useEffect and useState fetches without shared query deduplication.
Monolithic Deployment Bottleneck: Front-end releases were blocked by tightly coupled legacy Vue dependencies.
Lack of Optimistic Feedback: Analyst comments and tag updates felt sluggish due to waiting for full round-trip server confirmation.
sections.architecture: Replaced fragmented useEffect calls with a centralized TanStack Query layer featuring normalized query keys, automatic in-flight request deduplication, and tuned staleTime policies. Adopted the Strangler Fig pattern to progressively migrate legacy Vue.js KYB modules into modern TypeScript React micro-frontends with clear domain boundaries.
sections.implementation:
1. Normalized query caching across KYC, KYB, and AML alert widgets, sharing query results across sibling components.
2. Built optimistic UI mutations for Analyst Comments and Custom Views with automatic rollback on error.
3. Introduced Jest unit tests and Playwright E2E regression pipelines to safeguard each micro-frontend build.
results: 70% reduction in redundant network API calls across high-frequency analyst workflows
Independent domain deployments for AML, KYC/KYB, and Risk Investigations
Near-zero regression deployments backed by Playwright automated test suites
sections.lessons: Server state and client state require fundamentally different management patterns. Adopting TanStack Query as the single source of server truth vastly simplified state architecture compared to giant global Redux stores.

caseStudies.title: Architecting a Multi-Cloud FinOps Platform & Reusable SSE AI Chatbot
caseStudies.summary: Built high-performance cloud cost management dashboards with 1,000+ row virtualized tables and engineered a reusable, buffered SSE AI chatbot for real-time FinOps analysis.

sections.problem: Cloud FinOps dashboards ingest massive billing datasets across AWS, Azure, and GCP. Rendering 1,000+ rows of resource recommendations, power schedules, and multi-series charts caused severe browser frame drops on filter changes. Simultaneously, the platform required an AI FinOps advisor to answer complex billing queries without freezing the browser during token generation.
rootCause: DOM Overload: Rendering 1,000+ unvirtualized complex table rows with multiple data attributes overwhelmed browser layout engines.
Main-Thread Freezing during SSE: High-frequency token streaming (50-100 chunks/sec) triggered excessive React re-renders.
Redundant Metric Refetches: Switching between cloud account filters triggered identical billing queries repeatedly.
sections.architecture: Implemented DOM list virtualization for heavy billing tables and memoized chart computation pipelines. Engineered a hybrid RAG backend (Node.js + Pinecone vector search + Elasticsearch hybrid keyword retrieval) paired with a custom buffered SSE client that uses requestAnimationFrame to lock UI rendering at a silky 60 FPS.
sections.implementation:
1. Integrated TanStack Virtual for 1,000+ row resource tables, cutting DOM node count from 25,000+ to under 120.
2. Built a chunk-buffering queue using requestAnimationFrame so high-throughput AI tokens are flushed once per frame rather than on every raw network chunk.
3. Layered TanStack Query caching over GraphQL and REST endpoints to eliminate redundant dashboard queries.
results: 45% fewer redundant API calls across cloud billing dashboards
40% reduction in unnecessary React re-renders on complex analytics views
Smooth, locked 60 FPS scrolling on 1,000+ row virtualized tables during active AI streaming
sections.lessons: Batching and frame synchronization are paramount when dealing with high-frequency streaming AI outputs. Unthrottled setState per chunk quickly degrades even top-spec hardware.

caseStudies.title: Engineering @frankieone/one-sdk to 4,500+ Weekly npm Downloads
caseStudies.summary: Architected a schema-driven KYC/IDV client library distributed via npm, powering biometric capture, identity verification, and multi-country form flows for global banks.

sections.problem: FinTech enterprises integrating KYC, ID document capture, and biometric checks operate under vastly different regional compliance rules, custom branding constraints, and varied failure modes. Building bespoke onboarding flows for each enterprise client was unmaintainable and slowed sales cycles.
rootCause: Brittle Hardcoded Flows: Regional compliance requirements (e.g. Australian Medicare vs. US SSN vs. Indian Aadhaar) required completely different field validations.
Mobile Camera & Timeout Flakiness: High user drop-off during camera document capture due to unhandled network drops and camera permissions.
CSS Clashes: Host applications embedding the SDK experienced stylesheet bleed and styling conflicts.
sections.architecture: Architected a configuration-driven, schema-based dynamic form renderer that dynamically mounts verification steps, field rules, and 15+ calendar/date validation variants based on client JSON configs. Designed an isolated headless UI architecture with theme tokens so clients can customize styles without breaking core state machines.
sections.implementation:
1. Built a schema interpreter supporting nested conditionality, async field validation, and dynamic step sequences.
2. Implemented automated retry handling and resilient fallback state machines for flaky document captures and camera permissions.
3. Published strict TypeScript definitions with generics to guide client developers during integration.
results: Published and actively maintained at 4,500+ weekly downloads on npm across enterprise FinTech clients
60% reduction in client engineering onboarding integration time
Zero global CSS conflicts via scoped styling architecture
sections.lessons: Building developer-facing libraries requires far stricter API ergonomics, backward-compatibility discipline, and error telemetry than internal applications.

articles.title: Fixing React UI Freezes During High-Frequency SSE LLM Streaming
articles.subtitle: How requestAnimationFrame buffering eliminated 40ms frame drops when rendering 80+ tokens/sec
articles.summary: When your LLM streams 60-100 tokens per second, naive `setState` on every Server-Sent Event (SSE) chunk overwhelms React's render pipeline and drops framerates to 20 FPS. Here is how we locked 60 FPS using ref-based chunk accumulation and `requestAnimationFrame`.

articles.title: Simple Code vs. Over-Engineering: Why Clean Beats Clever in Production
articles.subtitle: The architectural traps that cost teams months of refactoring and how to avoid them
articles.summary: Clever code is a liability. Simple, predictable code is an asset. A breakdown of when abstractions help, when they destroy velocity, and why boring engineering wins in production.
articles.content:
### The Senior Engineer's Dilemma

Early in our careers, we measure our skill by how complex our solutions are. We introduce abstract factory patterns, premature micro-frontends, dynamic plugin architectures, and 5-layer Redux state trees for a 2-page form.

Seniority is realizing that **code is a liability, not an asset**. Every line of code written must be tested, debugged, read by colleagues, and maintained through major dependency upgrades.

### Three Over-Engineering Traps We Killed

1. **Giant Global State for Local Modals:** Putting `isModalOpen` into global Redux store instead of component state or URL search parameters.
2. **Custom Fetch Wrappers that Re-invent TanStack Query:** Writing 600 lines of homegrown caching, deduplication, and retry logic instead of using battle-tested libraries.
3. **Premature Micro-Frontends:** Splitting a 15k LOC app into 4 separate repositories before domain boundaries or team sizes justified the operational overhead.

### The Rule of Three

Do not create an abstraction until you have duplicated the exact pattern three times. When you do abstract, make sure the abstraction is easier to delete than the code it replaces.

articles.title: Dropping Next.js LCP from 7.0s to 1.2s with Route Splitting & Hydration Budgets
articles.subtitle: How we audited and eliminated 82% of load latency on a production legal SaaS
articles.summary: A deep dive into diagnosing render-blocking resources, implementing next/dynamic code splitting, and prioritizing hero imagery to pass Google Core Web Vitals.
articles.content:
### The 7-Second Problem

When we audited DigiLawyer AI, Chrome Lighthouse reported an alarming 7.0s LCP on mobile 4G networks. In consumer LegalTech, every additional second of latency increases drop-off by 20%.

### The Audit

Using Chrome DevTools Performance panel and WebPageTest:
1. The initial JavaScript bundle was 1.4MB compressed.
2. The hero image was loaded with `loading='lazy'` (never do this for the LCP element!).
3. Unused heavy libraries (PDF viewers, Quill editors) were imported at the top of the root layout.

### The Fixes

* **Priority Image Loading:** Marked the hero banner with `priority={true}` and provided exact `sizes` to eliminate layout shift.
* **Dynamic Imports with SSR False:** Moved document editors and canvas signatures behind `dynamic(() => import(...), { ssr: false })`.
* **Font Optimization:** Replaced external Google Fonts links with `next/font/google`, inlining font declarations at build time and eliminating a DNS round-trip.

**Result:** LCP dropped to 1.2s, Core Web Vitals passed across all mobile and desktop audits.

articles.title: Why URL State Beats Global Redux for Search, Filters, and Modals
articles.subtitle: Making state shareable, bookmarkable, and reload-proof using nuqs and searchParams
articles.summary: Stop putting filter state into Redux or useState. Moving search queries, active tabs, and pagination to URL query params unlocks shareability, browser history, and zero-state sync bugs.
articles.content:
### The Broken Refresh Problem

How many times have you carefully set 5 filters on a SaaS dashboard, hit refresh, and watched all your filters reset to default? Or copied a URL to Slack, only for your coworker to see a blank default screen?

This happens when developers store view parameters in React `useState` or Redux instead of the URL.

### The URL as Single Source of Truth

The URL is the original state store of the web. By binding your filter and pagination state to `URLSearchParams`:
1. **Shareability:** Every state configuration is a permanent link.
2. **Browser History:** Back and forward buttons work intuitively.
3. **Multi-Tab Workflows:** Opening a card in a new tab preserves its exact context.
4. **Zero Cache Sync:** When the user refreshes, the application immediately reads the URL and re-hydrates the exact view.
